author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
occasion: Gregory, after eight years of silence from rhetorical practice, during which he has only listened to philosophers, prepares to deliver a speech of thanks and praise to his teacher Origen, though he feels inadequate to the task.
argument: Gregory begins by confessing his long silence and lack of training in elegant Greek rhetoric, explaining that he has neither spoken nor written for eight years, and has only listened to philosophers who value accurate investigation over polished speech. He further explains that the Roman laws, though wise and admirable, are expressed in the Roman tongue, which is magnificent and suited to imperial majesty but personally difficult and burdensome for him to use. He compares skilled orators to painters with rich colors, while he is like a poor man painting with coals or broken pieces of greenware, using common words to represent the impressions of his mind. Finally, he says the very subject of his speech—a man who appears human, but to those who can perceive the greatness of his character and habits, seems endowed with greater and nearly divine ornaments—makes him hesitate and hold back.

outline.move: Gregory explains his long silence, his lack of rhetorical training, the difficulty of the subject, and his hesitation to speak about a man who seems almost divine.

cast.name: Origen
cast.who: The teacher and subject of the panegyric, described as a man who appears human, but to those who can perceive the greatness of his character and habits, seems endowed with greater and nearly divine ornaments.

key_terms.sense: The state of not speaking, which Gregory has maintained for eight years and which he now must break.
The pursuit of wisdom and truth, embraced by the admirable men Gregory mentions, who value accurate investigation over elegant speech.
The Roman laws that govern all subjects of the empire, described as wise, pious, varied, and admirable, but expressed in the difficult Roman tongue.
Speech or language, particularly the polished and elegant Greek rhetorical style Gregory lacks, and the difficult Roman tongue of the laws.
Words or utterances, described as images of the mind's concepts, which skilled speakers can paint with rich variety.
Painters, used as a metaphor for skilled orators who can depict their thoughts with rich colors and variety.
Coals or charcoal, used as a metaphor for the poor, common means with which Gregory must paint his thoughts.
Broken pieces of greenware or potsherds, used alongside coals as a metaphor for the poor, common materials with which Gregory must paint his thoughts.
Impressions or characters of the mind, which Gregory attempts to represent in his speech, though not clearly or elegantly.
Divine qualities or ornaments, with which the subject of the speech seems endowed, making Gregory hesitate to speak.

uncertain: The specific occasion or setting of the speech
Whether the 'admirable men' mentioned are a specific philosophical school or group

_unresolved_facts.claim: during which he has only listened to philosophers
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: nec alium audivi quem vel privatim scribentem, historiamve, vel publice panegyricos sermones, controversiasque declamantem, praeter hosce admirabiles viros, qui pulchram philosophiam amplexi sunt
_unresolved_facts.fix: during which he has only listened to these admirable men who have embraced true philosophy (not 'philosophers' in a general sense, but specifically these particular men)

_unresolved_facts.claim: the Roman laws, though wise and admirable, are expressed in the Roman tongue, which is magnificent and suited to imperial majesty but personally difficult and burdensome for him to use
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: mirificae nimirum leges nostrae, quibus omnium nunc, qui Romanorum imperio parent, res gubernantur... ceterum Romano expositae, traditaeque sermone, admirabili sane atque magnifico, et ad imperii maiestatem confirmato; sed mihi gravi nihilominus ac difficili
_unresolved_facts.fix: the Roman laws, which govern all now subject to Roman rule, are expressed in the Roman tongue, which is magnificent and suited to imperial majesty; but Gregory finds the study of these laws (not the language itself) personally difficult and burdensome—he says 'mihi gravi nihilominus ac difficili' referring to the laws, not the language per se

_unresolved_facts.claim: He compares skilled orators to painters with rich colors, while he is like a poor man painting with coals or broken pieces of greenware
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: tanquam solis carbonibus aut testulis viratorum, communiumque nominum ac verborum
_unresolved_facts.fix: He compares skilled orators to painters with rich colors, while he is like a poor man painting with coals or broken pieces of greenware (testulis viratorum—'potsherds of greenware' or 'glazed earthenware shards'), using common names and words

_unresolved_facts.claim: The speaker, a student preparing to praise his teacher Origen after eight years of silence from rhetorical practice
_unresolved_facts.fix: The speaker, a student preparing to praise his teacher Origen after eight years without giving or writing any speech, long or short, and without hearing anyone declaiming except the admirable men who embraced true philosophy
